titleStmt.title: SPET: Transparent SRAM Allocation and Model Partitioning for Real-time DNN Tasks on Edge TPU

analytic.title: SPET: Transparent SRAM Allocation and Model Partitioning for Real-time DNN Tasks on Edge TPU

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have been deployed in many safety-critical real-time embedded systems. To support DNN tasks in realtime, most previous studies focused on GPU or CPU. However, Edge TPU has not yet been studied for real-time guarantees. This paper presents a real-time DNNs framework for Edge TPU to satisfy multiple DNN inference tasks' timing requirements. The proposed framework provides 1) SRAM allocation and model partitioning techniques and 2) a MIPbased algorithm that determines the amount of SRAM and the number of segments for each task. The experiment result shows that our framework provides 79% higher schedulability than the existing Edge TPU system.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have shown tremendous success in many Internet-of-Things (IoT) and cyber-physical systems (CPS) such as autonomous driving [1], smart robotics [2], and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV) [3]. With the rapid increase in such on-device DNN workloads, specialized hardware accelerators are becoming an attractive solution to improve both performance and energy efficiency. For example, Google Edge Tensor Processing Units (Edge TPU) [4] and Apple Neural Engines [5] are already presented as essential hardware components in commodity embedded systems. Despite the advent of specialized DNN accelerators, there still exist several factors that cause long and unpredictable execution times of DNN tasks, limiting their deployment on real-time systems.

In this paper, we first examine the execution behavior of DNN tasks on a commercial DNN accelerator, Google Edge TPU, and reveal two major barriers to provide worst-case timing guarantees for real-time DNN tasks: B1) deadline-oblivious SRAM allocation and B2) non-preemptive nature without system-wide scheduling decision. Edge TPU features on-chip SRAM used as scratchpads to cache DNN model parameter data. Although Edge TPU allows multiple DNN tasks to share SRAM to improve the performance of DNN inference, the amount of SRAM allocated to each task is determined without considering its timing requirement. Our experimentation with popular DNN models on Edge TPU has demonstrated an up to 5.2x execution time difference by different amounts of SRAM allocation. Moreover, Edge TPU employs canonical scheduling principles (i.e., FIFO) that sequentially schedule DNN tasks in a non-preemptive manner without prioritizing them according to their timing constraints. Therefore, those two factors may impose long and unpredictable response times on DNN tasks, posing significant challenges to the efficient use of Edge TPU in meeting timing requirements.

Although some recent studies [6]- [9] have focused on ensuring the timing constraints of DNN tasks on GPU-accelerated hardware platforms and made valuable contributions, they did not deal with Edge TPU's inherent internal architecture, rendering them infeasible for Edge TPU. Different from GPU that supports programmable memory management, Edge TPU has limited flexibility in leveraging internal memory, highly relying on its closed-source compiler. Other studies [10]- [12] have focused on optimizing energy efficiency or computational throughput on hardware accelerators. However, these solutions did not deal with the timing constraints of DNN tasks. To the best of our knowledge, there is no prior work on Edge TPU to provide worst-case timing guarantees for real-time DNN tasks. * Sangeun Oh is the corresponding author.

We aim to guarantee and improve the schedulability of real-time DNN tasks on Edge TPU. To achieve this goal, we propose a new system abstraction, SPET (transparent and predictable SRAM allocation and model Partitioning for Edge TPU). One of the key features of SPET is a transparent SRAM allocation mechanism that offers maximum flexibility in allocating a dedicated amount of SRAM to each DNN task (addressing B1), without requiring any code modification of the Edge TPU compiler. Another key feature is an adaptive DNN model partitioning mechanism that provides predictable preemption points between smaller non-preemptive regions (addressing B2). The other key feature is the support of online system-wide scheduling decision according to tasks' priorities (addressing B2). Building upon the above three features, SPET develops a new policy that determines the allocation of SRAM and the number of model partitions for each DNN task in a way to improve schedulability. To this end, we derive a response time analysis to verify whether DNN tasks satisfy their timing constraints for a given SRAM allocation and model partitioning. We then formulate a mixed-integer programming (MIP) problem that takes into account the effect of each task's SRAM allocation and model partitioning on the schedulability with respect to the proposed schedulability analysis.

We implement SPET on top of TensorFlow Lite and evaluate its effectiveness with seven popular DNN models on the Google Coral Dev board. The evaluation results show that SPET makes up to 79% more real-time DNN task sets schedulable over the existing approaches. We also show, via a case study of emergency braking on a scaled self-driving car, that SPET can improve quality of control with timely inference, thus enhancing safety.
This paper makes the following main contributions:
• Identifying two major barriers to efficient use of Edge TPU for real-time DNN tasks to fulfill their timing requirements;
• Development of SPET, a new system abstraction that enables predictable SRAM allocation and scheduling on Edge TPU;
• Development of SRAM allocation and model partitioning algorithms that not only provide timing guarantees but also improve schedulability performance; and
• Demonstration of SPET's effectiveness, via in-depth evaluation and a case study, in terms of schedulability performance.

div.head: A. Background on Edge TPU
div.p: Edge TPU is a hardware accelerator designed by Google to run DNN tasks at the edge. Edge TPU is connected to host memory (i.e., DRAM) through the PCI bus, and its internal architecture is composed of processing elements (PEs) and cache memory called SRAM. The PEs are organized with a two-dimensional array structure, allowing parallel processing of arithmetic operations in a DNN model. SRAM, device memory with 8 MB size, can cache the model's parameter data, enabling faster inference than fetching the parameter data from host memory.

Edge TPU runs a DNN task with two phases, offline and online. In the offline phase, the Edge TPU compiler compiles the task's DNN model into a binary file compatible with Edge TPU. The compiler also determines the specific amount of the model's parameter data to be cached into SRAM at the layer-level granularity. In the online When multiple DNN tasks are executed on Edge TPU, the compiler supports co-compilation that allows them to share SRAM to cache their parameter data together. The amount of SRAM exclusively allocated to each task is fixed at compile time, and its location on SRAM is sequentially determined in the order the tasks appear in the compiler command. If all model parameter data of multiple tasks cannot fit into SRAM, only partial data is cached into SRAM, and it is prioritized based on how frequently each layer accesses the data.

div.head: B. Motivation
div.p: We now identify two significant barriers to the efficient use of Edge TPU so as to accommodate as many real-time DNN tasks as possible without violating any timing constraints.

Deadline-oblivious SRAM allocation. The Edge TPU compiler fails to consider the timing constraints of real-time DNN tasks since it employs a deadline-oblivious SRAM allocation approach that assigns SRAM in favor of frequently accessed layers regardless of the tasks' deadlines. Such a deadline-oblivious SRAM allocation approach would not be efficient in guaranteeing timing constraints. This is because the execution time of a DNN task on Edge TPU significantly varies depending on the amount of its model parameter data to be cached into SRAM. To demonstrate this issue, we conducted experiments to measure the execution times of representative DNN models (EfficientNet-{L,M,S}, MobileNetV2, and ResNet) on the Edge TPU of the Google Coral dev board [13]. As shown in Fig. 1(a), our experimental results show that the execution time of each DNN model is decreased as its SRAM allocation size increases. For example, executing EfficientNet-S without SRAM allocation yields a slowdown of 5.2× over executing it with the maximum SRAM allocation. Such execution time variations according to SRAM allocation differ by different DNN models. This calls for deadline-aware SRAM allocation for Edge TPU; an SRAM allocation mechanism must determine the amounts of SRAM allocated to tasks by taking into account both different execution times depending on their SRAM allocation and timing constraints to accommodate as many real-time DNN tasks as possible without violating any timing constraints.

Non-preemptive nature of Edge TPU. Edge TPU uses canonical scheduling principles (i.e., FIFO) that sequentially schedule DNN tasks in a non-preemptive manner without prioritizing them according to their timing constraints. Due to the non-preemptive nature of Edge TPU, a high-priority task can be blocked by a currently-executing low-priority task. Such a blocking effect may impose an unpredictable shows an empirical CDF (cumulative distribution function) of the execution delay when running three tasks together on a vanilla Edge TPU (nonpreemptive FIFO) for 10 seconds; tasks τ1, τ2, and τ3 make inference requests for EfficientNet-L, EfficientNet-M, and MobileNetV2 every 100ms, 50ms, 30ms. Every task suffer from long and unpredictable execution delays over a wide range from 0.03ms to 395.75ms. This calls for a new system-wide scheduler for Edge TPU; a system-wide scheduler must provide priority-based scheduling and predictable preemption points with smaller non-preemptive regions to efficiently utilize Edge TPU in meeting timing requirements.

To demonstrate how the above-mentioned features can adversely affect schedulability, let us consider a task set with the following two tasks: τ1 and τ2 use MobileNetV2 and EfficientNet-L with the deadline of 10ms and 45ms, respectively. Consider the scheduling scenario shown in Fig. 2. We compare (a) vanilla Edge TPU and (b) SPET. Under vanilla Edge TPU, SRAM is preferentially allocated to EfficientNet-L (5.5MB) rather than MobileNetV2 (1.6MB) because EfficientNet-L has the model parameter data accessed more frequently than MobileNetV2. This causes a deadline miss of the first inference request of τ1 as shown in Fig 2(a) due to a longer execution time (12ms) than its deadline (10ms). The second inference request of τ1 also misses its deadline due to a long blocking delay by τ2. In contrast to vanilla Edge TPU, SPET allocates more SRAM to MobileNetV2 (3.9MB) by considering its deadline, resulting in no deadline miss of the first inference request of τ1. SPET also supports priority-based scheduling 1 and preemption points at boundaries between smaller non-preemptive regions by splitting each DNN model into multiple segments, resulting in no deadline miss of the second inference request of τ2. Therefore, it is important to address both two barriers in leveraging Edge TPU to improve schedulability.

div.head: A. System Overview
div.p: Due to the factors mentioned above, it is challenging for Edge TPU to guarantee and improve the schedulability of real-time DNN tasks. The execution time of a task on Edge TPU varies depending on the amount of its model parameter data cached into SRAM. Thus, it is important to decide and allocate the "right" amount of parameter data on SRAM for each individual task while preserving feasibility. However, SRAM allocation relies upon the deadline-oblivious and closed-source Edge TPU compiler, which hinders deadline-aware and flexible SRAM allocation. In addition, the amount of interference or blocking delay imposed by other tasks may also vary depending on the schedule of tasks to be executed on Edge TPU, both of which affect the response time of a DNN task. However, Edge TPU sequentially schedules DNN tasks in a non-preemptive FIFO manner without considering tasks' different timing constraints, which yields unpredictable delays and is difficult to guarantee the schedulability of real-time DNN tasks. To address those challenges, we propose a new system abstraction, named SPET, that enables transparent and predictable SRAM allocation and scheduling of real-time DNN tasks for Edge TPU. The core design features of SPET include Flexible SRAM allocator, DNN model partitioner, and System-wide scheduler as depicted in Fig. 3. Both Flexible SRAM allocator and DNN model partitioner are tightly coupled with the Edge TPU compiler in the offline phase and play key roles in allocating a dedicated amount of SRAM to each individual task and providing predictable preemption points between smaller nonpreemptive regions, respectively. In particular, Flexible SRAM allocator properly utilizes auxiliary DNN models in combination with the cocompilation feature of the Edge TPU compiler. As a result, Flexible SRAM allocator can allocate a portion of SRAM with a particular size and location to a target DNN model without requiring any code modification of the DNN model and additional space overhead. DNN model partitioner splits a target DNN model into multiple segments so that preemption points appear at segment boundaries. Systemwide scheduler supports priority-based scheduling that automatically orchestrates the execution and preemption of tasks according to their priority in the online phase to meet the timing constraints.

Building upon the above three features, SPET develops a new scheduling policy that determines the SRAM allocation and the number of segments for each DNN task in a way to improve schedulability. To this end, we derive a response time analysis to verify whether DNN tasks satisfy their timing constraints with careful consideration of the effect of each task's SRAM allocation and model partitioning on the execution time, interference delay, and blocking delay. We then formulate SRAM allocation and model partitioning as a mixed-integer programming (MIP) problem subject to the proposed response time analysis.

div.head: B. Design of SPET
div.p: SPET supports transparent SRAM allocation and scheduling for DNN tasks on Edge TPU while providing real-time guarantees, without having to modify the code of DNN models. We now describe the design details of SPET.

Flexible SRAM allocator. We describe how Flexible SRAM allocator allocates a dedicated amount of SRAM to each DNN task on Edge TPU. If we compile multiple DNN models separately without co-compilation, each model can exclusively utilize the entire SRAM to cache its model parameter data while running. In compilation, the Edge TPU compiler gives each model a unique caching token. Upon an inference request for a DNN model, the Edge TPU runtime compares its token to the currently cached token. If the tokens match, the runtime uses the cached data. If they do not match, it flushes the entire SRAM and loads the requested model's data to SRAM, imposing significant overhead. If we use the co-compilation feature of the Edge TPU compiler, multiple models can share SRAM, eliminating the flushing and re-loading overhead. However, we cannot control the size and location of SRAM allocated to each individual DNN model due to the proprietary black box Edge TPU compiler. To solve this conflicting issue, Flexible SRAM allocator exploits dummy DNN models jointly with the co-compilation feature. Basically, for a given amount of SRAM allocated to each task, Flexible SRAM allocator sequentially assigns SRAM to tasks, one by one, with separate co-compilation as described in Fig. 4. For each task's SRAM allocation, it is co-compiled with at most two dummy DNN models. Those dummy DNN models consist of the layers with the most frequently accessed so that they are guaranteed to allocate all data to SRAM according to the default SRAM allocation policy of the Edge TPU compiler. Flexible SRAM allocator then can allocate the dedicated size and location of SRAM to each task by properly setting the size of dummy DNN model(s) and the co-compile order of dummy and target DNN models. Consider that we want a task τi to be allocated on SRAM with size s * i and offset fi, where s * i is determined by the proposed MIP-based algorithm (to be discussed in Sec. IV) and fi = i j=1 s * j 2 . Flexible SRAM allocator sets the sizes of two dummy DNN models (referred to as s d1 and s d2 ) to s d1 = fi and s d2 = M -s d1 -s * i , where M is the total size of SRAM, and co-compiles in the order of s d1 , s * i , and s d2 . As an example shown in Fig. 4, out of 8MB SRAM size, τ2 is allocated on SRAM with size s * 2 = 4MB and offset f2 = 2MB by co-compiling two dummy DNN models-the first one with size s d1 = 2MB and the second one with size s d2 = 2MB-in the order of s d1 , s * 2 , and s d2 . Note that Flexible SRAM allocator only needs a single dummy DNN model s d2 = M -s * 1 to allocate τ1 with size s * 1 . Likewise, τn can be allocated to SRAM with size s * n with a single dummy DNN model s d1 = M -s * n , where n is the number of tasks. By setting the offset of each task τi to fi = i j=1 s * j , it is guaranteed that each portion of SRAM allocated to each task does not overlap each other.

By repeating such co-compilation for all tasks, Flexible SRAM allocator can generate executable binary files that specify the size and location of SRAM allocated to each task. Since each task is co-compiled only with its corresponding dummy DNN models separately from the other tasks, each task's binary file has a different token from each other. To prevent from unnecessary flushing and reloading overhead, Flexible SRAM allocator automatically instruments the generated binary files so that they are assigned the same caching token. As a result, Flexible SRAM allocator enables transparent and flexible SRAM allocation of each DNN task on Edge TPU, without requiring any modification of the (closed-source) Edge TPU compiler.

DNN model partitioner. DNN model partitioner splits a target DNN model into multiple segments to provide preemption points at boundaries between the segments. Hence, the blocking delay of a high-priority task is bounded by the maximum time to execute a segment in lower-priority tasks. When the number of segments (referred to as g * i ) for each task τi is determined by the proposed MIP-based algorithm (to be discussed in Sec. IV), the sequence of τi's layers should be split into g * i segments so that the total execution time is evenly divided among the segments, thus minimizing the maximum blocking time. One issue is that the execution time of 2 We assume that tasks are indexed according to the order of co-compilation. each layer varies depending on SRAM allocation, i.e., whether its model parameter data is cached or not. Another issue is that there exists segmentation overhead. When the preemption of a high-priority task happens after the completion of a currently-executing segment of a lower-priority task, the output data of the currently-executing segment should be copied to host memory (i.e., download copy).

Then, the output data should be transferred back to device memory (i.e., upload copy) to be used as input to the successive segment when scheduled. Such upload and download copy overheads depend on which layer is located at the end of each segment. We refer to the layer located at the end of each segment as a segment boundary. Thus, we need to consider those two issues together when determining segment boundaries to minimize the maximum blocking time.

To this end, for a given SRAM allocation s * i and number of segments g * i , DNN model partitioner maintains each DNN's profile including its execution time and upload/download copy cost at layer level. According to those profiles, DNN model partitioner determines the segment boundaries of g * i -1 segments except the last one as follows. System-wide scheduler. System-wide scheduler supports prioritybased scheduling and segment-level preemption. System-wide scheduler runs as a background daemon to communicate with DNN tasks via inter-process communication (IPC). The scheduler maintains each segment's binary file and a priority queue for scheduling segments according to their priorities. When a segment finishes its execution, it sends a complete message to the scheduler, which then dequeues the highest priority segment from the queue.

div.head: IV. MIP-BASED ALGORITHM
div.p: In this section, we first describe our target system model with notations. We then derive a response time analysis that determines the schedulability of a set of real-time DNN tasks under any given SRAM allocation and model partitioning. Finally, we develop a MIP formulation that finds the SRAM allocation size and the number of segments for each task, which yields the schedulability of the task set by the response time analysis.

div.head: A. System Model and Notations
div.p: Real-time DNN inference tasks are presented as the sporadic task model widely used in various real-time systems. We assume each task uses a single DNN model and makes one inference request per job. Each DNN task τi ∈ τ can be specified as τi = (Ti, Ni, Si, Gi, Ci, Oi), where Ti is the minimum separation between successive job releases (equal to the deadline of τi), and Ni is the number of layers. The other parameters are dependent on SRAM allocation and model partitioning of τi. Si is a set of possible SRAM sizes allocated to τi and is specified as Si = {s min i , ..., s max i }, where s min i and s max i are the minimum (no) and maximum SRAM sizes to be allocated to τi, respectively. An element in between s min i and s max i in Si is determined as a multiple of the minimum allocatable SRAM size, i.e., 70KB. Gi is a set of possible values of the number of segments for τi and is specified as Gi = {1 ≤ gi ≤ Ni}, where gi = 1 and gi = Ni are the cases of no partitioning and all layers belonging to separate segments, respectively. Ci is the cumulative worst-case execution time (WCET) of τi that depends on the allocated SRAM size and is specified as Ci = {Ci(si)s i ∈S i }. Oi is the cumulative worstcase upload/download copy overhead to transfer the input/output of τi that depends on both the allocated SRAM size and the number of segments and is specified as Oi = {Oi(si, gi)s i ∈S i ,g i ∈G i }. Note that the values of Ci and Oi can be estimated from DNN profiles obtained by a measurement-based approach.

We consider task-level fixed-priority scheduling where each task has a static priority shared over all its segments. Execution of each segment is non-preemptive, so the preemption of a higher-priority task is permitted only after completing the currently-executing segment of a lower-priority task. We assume a quantum-based time; let one time unit a quantum length without loss of generality.

div.head: B. Response Time Analysis and MIP Formulation
div.p: We state the SRAM allocation and model partitioning problem. Definition 1 (SRAM Allocation and Model Partitioning): Given a task set τ and an Edge TPU platform, find i) an SRAM allocation size s * i and ii) a segment count g * i for each DNN task τi ∈ τ such that all tasks meet their deadlines under fixed-priority scheduling.

To solve the above problem, we first develop a response time analysis to derive an upper bound on the worst-case response time (WCRT) of a DNN task by taking into account the effect of SRAM allocation and model partitioning on the WCRT. We then formulate the SRAM allocation and model partitioning problem as an optimization problem subject to the necessary conditions including the proposed response time analysis.

Response time analysis. For concise presentation, Λi denotes a given pair of the SRAM size and the number of segments (si, gi) for τi. For a given SRAM allocation and model partitioning Λ = {{Λi}τ i ∈τ }, the WCRT wi(Λ) of each task τi ∈ τ under task-level fixed-priority scheduling can be calculated as
div.formula: w i (Λ) = C i (s i ) + O i (Λ i ) + I i (T i , Λ) + B i (Λ)(1)
div.p: where Ii(Ti, Λ) is the cumulative interference on the segments in τi caused by higher-priority tasks and Bi(Λ) is the blocking delay of the first segment in τi caused by a lower-priority task. Note that only the first segment in each task can be blocked by a currentlyexecuting segment of a lower-priority task under task-level fixedpriority scheduling.

Let hp(τi) be the set of all tasks with higher priority than τi. The segments of τi can be delayed by the segments of higher-priority tasks τ h . The number of jobs of τ h released during the deadline Ti of a single job of τi is at most (1 + ⌊ T i T h ⌋). Then, the cumulative interference Ii(Ti, Λ) on τi is upper-bounded by
div.formula: I i (T i , Λ) = τ h ∈hp(τ i ) (1 + ⌊ T i T h ⌋) • (C h (s h ) + O h (Λ h )).(2)
div.p: Let lp(τi) be the set of all tasks with lower priority than τi. In addition to the cumulative interference, a task τi can be further blocked by the currently-executing segment of a lower-priority task τ l . The blocking delay Bi is upper-bounded by
div.formula: B i (Λ) = max p:τ l ∈lp(τ i )∧1≤p≤g l (C p l (Λ l ) + O p l (Λ l ) -1)(3)
div.p: where C p l (Λ l ) and O p l (Λ l ) are the execution time and upload/download copy overhead of the p-th segment in τ l for a given Λ l , respectively.
Then, we can check the schedulability of a task set τ as presented in the following lemma:
Lemma 1: For a given SRAM allocation and model partitioning Λ, a task set τ is schedulable under task-level fixed-priority scheduling if ∀τi ∈ τ, wi(Λ) ≤ Ti.

Proof: There are at most (1 + ⌊ T i T h ⌋) jobs of any τ h ∈ τ that can be executed within an interval of length Ti. Then, the maximum cumulative interference on τi in the interval Ti is upper-bounded by Eq. ( 2). In addition, a task τi is blocked at most once by one segment of a lower-priority task, so the maximum blocking time on τi is upper-bounded by Eq. ( 3). This means wi(Λ) of Eq. ( 1) is an upper-bound of the response time of τi's jobs, and they complete their execution within wi(Λ) in any case. Therefore, if wi(Λ) ≤ Ti holds for all τi ∈ τ , τ is schedulable.

MIP formulation. We formulate the SRAM allocation and model partitioning as a MIP problem subject to our response time analysis. We first define 0/1 decision variables {x k i } and {y j i } which correspond to k-th possible SRAM size in Si and j-th possible segment count in Gi for each task τi, respectively. x k i is assigned as 1 if s * i is selected as k-th element in Si and assigned as 0 otherwise. y j i is assigned as 1 if g * i is selected as j-th element in Gi and assigned as 0 otherwise. Then, we find the solution {(s * i , g * i )τ i ∈τ } that satisfies the following four constraints (C1-C4):
div.formula: C1 : ∀τ i ∈ τ, 1≤k≤|S i | x k i = 1, C2 : ∀τ i ∈ τ, 1≤j≤|G i | y j i = 1 C3 : τ i ∈τ 1≤k≤|S i | s k i • x k i ≤ M , C4 : ∀τ i ∈ τ, w i (Λ) ≤ T i ,(4)
div.p: where M is the total SRAM size. Constraints C1 and C2 specify that one value from each of Si and Gi must be chosen for each task τi, respectively. Constraint C3 specifies that the sum of the amount of SRAM allocated to each task must not exceed the total SRAM size M . Constraint C4 specifies that τi's WCRT must not exceed its deadline Ti according to the response time analysis. We solve the MIP formulation using a well-known commercial MIP solver, Gurobi [14]. The resulting values of s * i and g * i indicate the SRAM allocation and segment count for τi to be used by Flexible SRAM allocator and DNN model partitioner.

div.head: V. EVALUATION
div.p: We demonstrate the capability of SPET to make a significant improvement in schedulability for Edge TPU.

Experimental setup. We have implemented and evaluated SPET on top of TensorFlow Lite, one of the state-of-the-art embedded DNN frameworks. DNNs designed with TensorFlow Lite are easily adapted to SPET because SPET does not require any modification to the software stack of Edge TPU. For evaluation, we use seven popular DNN models for image classification (EfficientNet-{L,M,S}, Approaches to be compared. We compare the following seven different approaches:
• SPET: SPET with all components;
• SPET w/o MP: SPET without DNN model partitioner;
• SPET w/o SA: SPET without Flexible SRAM allocator;

• DPSA: deadline-proportional SRAM allocation only; It allocates SRAM to tasks in inverse proportion to their deadlines, so a task with shorter deadline gets more SRAM space; and • Base-Seg{1, 2, 6}: default (deadline-oblivious) SRAM allocation and static model partitioning; The number of segments of each task is set to 1, 2, or 6 according to the postfix of the approach name. Note that Base-Seg1 is vanilla Edge TPU (also indicated by Base).

Evaluation result. We first show the extensive simulation results for synthetic task sets with randomly generated parameters. We use schedulability ratio as a performance metric. It is defined as the ratio of schedulable task sets to the total number of generated task sets. We randomly generate 8,500 task sets by using the UUniFast algorithm [15], which has been widely used for the generation of realtime task sets. Each task set includes eight DNN tasks whose DNN models are randomly selected among five image classification models. The worst-case execution time and upload/download copy overhead of each task are profiled on our target hardware, Google Coral. Each task's priority is determined by deadline-monotonic (DM) [16].

Fig. 6(a) compares the schedulability ratios with varying the total utilization rate Uτ of a task set from 0.2 to 1.0, where Uτ is defined as i ( s i ∈S i Ci(si)/|Si|)/Ti. SPET exhibits high capability in finding schedulable task sets in that SPET finds 34%, 42%, 69%, and 79% more schedulable task sets than Base-Seg2, Base-Seg6, DPSA, and Base-Seg1, respectively. The performance gap between SPET and the other approaches becomes larger as Uτ increases.

We further analyze how much portion each component in SPET contributes to schedulability improvement. We first compare different SRAM allocation approaches: SPET w/o MP, DPSA, and Base-Seg1. SPET w/o MP finds 16% and 23% more schedulable task sets than DPSA and Base-Seg1, respectively. The difference between SPET w/o MP and Base-Seg1 shows the improvement of allowing deadlineaware flexible SRAM allocation, compared to the Base-Seg1 case of deadline-oblivious SRAM allocation. Such an improvement grows when Uτ increases. This is because there are more cases where tasks with higher utilization cannot satisfy their timing constraints without careful SRAM allocation. DPSA also does not carefully We also compare different model partitioning approaches: SPET w/o SA and Base-Seg{6, 2, 1}. SPET w/o SA shows 13%, 7%, and 41% better schedulability than Base-Seg{6, 2, 1}, respectively. The difference between SPET w/o SA and Base-Seg1 shows the improvement of allowing preemption points at boundaries between segments, compared to the case where no preemption is allowed.

Base-Seg2 and Base-Seg6 cannot dominate each other, i.e., Base-Seg6 outperforms Base-Seg2 when Uτ < 0.55, but their performance is reversed when Uτ ≥ 0.55. This is because there exists a trade-off between blocking delay and copy overhead in determining the number of segments. A larger number of segments imposes less blocking delay on a high-priority task at the expense of high copy overhead. As Uτ increases, each task is more likely to have high utilization, which cannot accommodate high copy overhead. Thus, Base-Seg6 shows worse schedulability performance than Base-Seg2. However, SPET adaptively determines the number of segments for each task by considering such a trade-off, resulting in better performance than both approaches.

Next, we varied the number of tasks in a task set to identify its effect on schedulability. We generate 5,500 additional task sets in total while varying the number of tasks from 3 to 13 when Uτ = 0.7 as shown in Fig. 6(b). SPET is shown to outperform the other approaches for all values of the number of tasks. One remarkable observation is that the predominance between SPET w/o SA and SPET w/o MP changes as the number of tasks varies. As the number of tasks decreases, each task is more likely to have higher utilization. In this case, model partitioning is more effective in making the task deemed schedulable by reducing its blocking delay. Thus, SPET w/o SA outperforms SPET w/o MP when the number of tasks is less than 10. On the other hand, as the number of tasks increases, it becomes more critical to allocate a proper SRAM size to each task due to insufficient SRAM space. Thus, SPET w/o MP outperforms SPET w/o SA when the number of tasks is greater than 10. SPET tightly integrates both SRAM allocation and model partitioning, resulting in better schedulability in any case.

Case study: emergency braking. We deployed SPET into a scaled self-driving car (PiCar-V) equipped with a Raspberry Pi 3 B+ board, an Edge TPU USB accelerator, and a front camera to perform a case study of emergency braking. 4 We executed the following three tasks simultaneously: τ1(T1 = 250 ms, EfficientDet) for object detection, τ2(330 ms, DAVE-2) for lane tracking, and τ3(1,000 ms, InceptionV2) for image classification. In this experiment, the car moves toward straight along the road at 1.0m/s and the braking is activated as soon as a pedestrian is detected. And the camera's fieldof-view is limited to 1.0m to fix the point to perceive the pedestrian. Fig. 7(a) shows the average stopping distances for SPET and Base (plotted as bars) with a breakdown of the distance up to the detection point (perception-reaction) and the actual braking distance out of 10 trials. Base makes a braking decision at 1.0m and stops at 1.1m on average, exceeding the safe distance. The worst-case stopping distance is 1.8m. In contrast, SPET makes a braking decision at 0.3m and stops at 0.5m on average within the safe distance. The distance up to detection is reduced by 70% compared to Base. The worst-case stopping distance is 0.7m, which is still safe, demonstrating enhanced safety in a real-world environment. For detailed analysis, Fig. 7(b) and (c) show the response time CDF of the three tasks for Base and SPET, respectively, in the case study. Under Base, τ1 and τ2 show the maximum response times of 500ms and 399ms respectively and miss their deadlines, which leads to the pedestrian crash. In contrast, under SPET, τ1 and τ2 have the maximum response times of 239ms and 317ms respectively, making all tasks schedulable. This is because SPET performs SRAM allocation and model partitioning considering the deadlines of the three tasks, unlike Base.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: This paper aims to improve the schedulability of real-time DNN tasks on Edge TPU. We first revealed the technical barriers inherent in Edge TPU to support real-time guarantees. We then developed SPET that enables flexible SRAM allocation and model partitioning with consideration of timing constraints. Our evaluation results showed the effectiveness of SPET in meeting timing constraints. In the future, we would like to extend SPET to utilize multiple Edge TPUs.

Fig.1(b)shows an empirical CDF (cumulative distribution function) of the execution delay when running three tasks together on a vanilla Edge TPU (nonpreemptive FIFO) for 10 seconds; tasks τ1, τ2, and τ3 make inference requests for EfficientNet-L, EfficientNet-M, and MobileNetV2 every 100ms, 50ms, 30ms. Every task suffer from long and unpredictable execution delays over a wide range from 0.03ms to 395.75ms. This calls for a new system-wide scheduler for Edge TPU; a system-wide scheduler must provide priority-based scheduling and predictable preemption points with smaller non-preemptive regions to efficiently utilize Edge TPU in meeting timing requirements.To demonstrate how the above-mentioned features can adversely affect schedulability, let us consider a task set with the following two tasks: τ1 and τ2 use MobileNetV2 and EfficientNet-L with the deadline of 10ms and 45ms, respectively. Consider the scheduling scenario shown in Fig.2. We compare (a) vanilla Edge TPU and (b) SPET. Under vanilla Edge TPU, SRAM is preferentially allocated to EfficientNet-L (5.5MB) rather than MobileNetV2 (1.6MB) because EfficientNet-L has the model parameter data accessed more frequently than MobileNetV2. This causes a deadline miss of the first inference request of τ1 as shown in Fig2(a) due to a longer execution time (12ms) than its deadline (10ms). The second inference request of τ1 also misses its deadline due to a long blocking delay by τ2. In contrast to vanilla Edge TPU, SPET allocates more SRAM to MobileNetV2 (3.9MB) by considering its deadline, resulting in no deadline miss of the first inference request of τ1. SPET also supports priority-based scheduling1 and preemption points at boundaries between smaller non-preemptive regions by splitting each DNN model into multiple segments, resulting in no deadline miss of the second inference request of τ2. Therefore, it is important to address both two barriers in leveraging Edge TPU to improve schedulability.
